analysis.one_liner: Cracks down on for-profit colleges that manipulate loan default rates, mislead students, or go bankrupt with federal money.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the Senate HELP Committee on September 29, 2015 and died there when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let the Education Department go after colleges that game federal loan statistics — recalculating their true default rates, fining schools up to millions of dollars based on how risky their student bodies are, and using those fines to compensate defrauded students. It would have also made executives of for-profit colleges personally liable when their schools collapse and stick the government with discharged student loans. The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Students at career colleges that overstate job placement and graduation outcomes, and federal taxpayers who currently eat the cost when for-profit schools fail and their loans are discharged. The bill would also give state attorneys general a new tool to win refunds for defrauded students.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Education Department to recalculate a school's loan default rate — and re-examine whether it should keep federal aid eligibility — if the school used tricks like serial forbearance, reshuffling campuses, or changes of ownership to hide how many students default.
Lets the Education Department impose civil penalties starting at $100,000 and scaling up to $3 million multiplied by a school's student default risk, with repeat violations escalating.
Creates a Student Relief Fund out of penalty collections to give money back to students enrolled at schools that were sanctioned or broke federal student-aid rules.

Lets the Department hold executives of for-profit colleges personally liable for taxpayer and student losses tied to enforcement actions, and pursue executives and board members to recover discharged student loans.
Bars people found guilty of defrauding students from serving as officers or board members of for-profit colleges, and lets state attorneys general sue in federal court for restitution and refunds.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit college owners, executives, and boards, who would face fines scaled to their schools' default rates, personal liability for enforcement losses, a ban on convicted student-fraud perpetrators in their leadership, and being sued to repay discharged loans.

drawbacks.text: Penalties up to $3 million multiplied by a school's default risk, plus personal liability for executives, could push struggling for-profit schools into sudden closure, leaving enrolled students stranded mid-program — a real risk even if the schools were misbehaving.

The bill's harshest provisions apply mainly to for-profit colleges, so the sector could fairly argue it is targeted by party-line legislation rather than a rule applying evenly to all schools with poor outcomes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits — penalties that scale with a school's default footprint, personal liability for executives, and a relief fund for defrauded students — target the schools most likely to leave students with worthless credentials and federal debt. The strongest good-faith objection is that large, automatically escalating penalties and personal liability could push marginal for-profit schools into closure, leaving students stranded mid-program (the very 2015-16 collapses of Corinthian and ITT showed how disruptive sudden shutdowns can be). An honest supporter would acknowledge that even so, the alternative — students holding non-dischargeable federal debt from a school that hid its default rates — is worse.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate education committee, and it never came up again — no hearing, no vote, nothing — so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Murphy introduced S. 2098 on September 29, 2015 with four Democratic cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day — the only action the Senate ever took.
The committee held no markup and reported no version; the bill never reached the Senate floor for a vote.
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit college operators, whose executives stayed shielded from personal liability and whose default-rate tricks faced no new federal penalty.

for.name: Sen. Chris Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred to committee.

for.name: Sens. Durbin, Warren, Brown, and Blumenthal

against.name: For-profit college industry
against.what_they_did: The for-profit college sector, an active lobbying presence in Washington, opposed the broader Obama-era crackdown on career colleges; no group is recorded in the provided sources as acting on this bill.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in the fifteen months after it was referred.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill received no Republican support in a chamber where 54 Republicans held the majority.

industries.note: The bill imposed large civil penalties, personal liability for executives, loss of the default-rate escape hatch, and a fraud ban on officers — aimed squarely at schools whose students default on federal loans at high rates. Students and taxpayers, not the industry, would have gained.

industries.industry: Executives and board members of for-profit colleges
industries.note: Executives could have been personally billed for losses tied to enforcement actions and pursued for repaying discharged loans, ending the protection of hiding behind the corporate structure.

industries.industry: Federal student loan taxpayers (public at large)
industries.note: Taxpayers and students currently absorb loan discharges when schools collapse or defraud students; the bill shifted that recovery onto the executives and boards responsible.
